column2: The latest reading is an extremely strong forecast for the next 1 to 3 hours; the learned models add very little there.
column3: Autocorrelation 0.62 at 1 h. Final-model MAE skill vs persistence on test: 1 h +1.6% (interval +0.8% to +2.2%), 3 h +2.8% (interval +1.9% to +3.4%). On validation no model beats persistence at 1 h.
column4: For planning within about 3 hours, use the latest reading (persistence) as the forecast; do not spend effort deploying a model for this range.
column5: Zero modelling cost and no pipeline risk for short-range outlooks; effort is better spent on sensor uptime.
column6: One sensor, a few weeks of test data, small gains with approximate intervals.

column2: At 6 hours ahead a regularised linear model that predicts the change from the latest reading clearly improves on persistence.
column3: 6 h test MAE 8.84 vs persistence 10.97; skill +19.5% (interval +11.9% to +26.8%). Chosen by cross-validation before test.
column4: Use the 6 h model as a decision aid for next-shift planning (for example scheduling outdoor work), always shown next to the latest reading.
column5: The only horizon where analytics adds measurable planning value in this data.
column6: Test R² is -0.12 (negative), so level errors remain large; the test period is shifted upward (mean 35.4 vs 17.5 in training).

column2: Wind direction and lagged daily weather give little dependable benefit.
column3: In the ablation, adding wind or weather never meets the evidence rule. EDA: raw wind-sector medians differ by 18.4 µg/m³, but this is confounded with time of year and does not carry over once PM2.5 history is known; lagged-rain correlations are small.
column4: Do not build a data feed for these two inputs on the strength of this study; test hourly wind speed and satellite or hotspot data before investing.
column5: Avoids integration cost for a feature set that has not shown value.
column6: Daily weather comes from another station; the wind station is unknown; only April to August is covered.

column2: Forecast errors are far larger when PM2.5 is high, and there are too few such hours to judge.
column3: Test hours above 55 µg/m³ with the final models: 1 h: 16 hours, MAE 31.6 vs 4.2 on other hours; 3 h: 16 hours, MAE 35.2 vs 7.2 on other hours; 6 h: 15 hours, MAE 40.8 vs 7.6 on other hours.
column4: Do not use these forecasts to trigger health or operational alerts; keep official alerts and human judgement for high-pollution periods.
column5: Limits the tool to routine planning; avoids false reassurance during pollution episodes.
column6: Very few high hours and episodes; the October haze season is not in the data.

column2: PM2.5 levels drifted upward from training to test, so a model trained once will go stale.
column3: Mean target 17.5 µg/m³ in training vs 35.4 in test; the test-period R² is negative at 3 h and 6 h.
column4: Retrain on a rolling window (for example monthly) and track MAE against persistence each week.
column5: A small recurring maintenance task is needed if the 6 h model is used.
column6: Only five months; seasonality cannot be separated from drift.
